blockMcqs.question: In one phrase, what is dynamic programming?
options: Recursion plus reuse of cached subproblems
Always greedily taking the best local choice
blockMcqs.explanation: It trades memory for time by solving each distinct subproblem only once.

blockMcqs.question: Which pair of properties signals a DP problem?
options: Independent subproblems and a balanced tree
blockMcqs.explanation: Overlap makes caching pay off; optimal substructure makes the recurrence correct.

blockMcqs.question: Why is naive recursive Fibonacci exponential?
options: It allocates a new array every call
It recomputes the same subproblems repeatedly
Recursion is inherently slower than loops
blockMcqs.explanation: Only n+1 distinct values exist; the blow-up is all duplicate work.

blockMcqs.question: What is a DP "state"?
options: The order in which cells are filled
The minimal facts identifying a subproblem
The final answer cell of the table
blockMcqs.explanation: It must capture everything affecting the subproblem so its answer can be cached.

blockMcqs.question: Memoized Fibonacci's time and space are:
options: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
blockMcqs.explanation: Each of the n+1 states is computed once; the cache and stack each hold ~n.

blockMcqs.question: Why can 1D Fibonacci tabulation use O(1) space?
options: The array is reused across calls
Each value depends only on the last two
blockMcqs.explanation: Older cells are never read again, so two rolling variables suffice.

blockMcqs.question: What is the House Robber transition?
blockMcqs.explanation: At each house you take the better of skipping it or robbing it plus dp[i-2].

blockMcqs.question: Why does greedy fail on coin change but DP works?
options: Greedy can't handle a zero amount
Greedy needs all coins to be powers of two
Grabbing the largest coin can strand you short
blockMcqs.explanation: DP tries every coin at each amount, so a locally-best pick can't mislead it.
